title: "Drift"
description: "Has the model's performance changed since it was validated, and can we tell before the claims come in? PSI, domain classifiers and confidence-based performance estimation on simulated drift."

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

from modelperf.drift import (
    BATCH_SIZE,
    DIESEL_SHARE,
    N_MONTHS,
    RURAL_AREAS,
    RURAL_CLAIM_INCREASE,
    SCENARIOS,
    reference_and_pool,
    simulate_months,
)
from modelperf.metrics import (
    auc_rank,
    cbpe,
    domain_classifier_auc,
    log_loss,
    paired_bootstrap,
    population_stability_index,
    psi_table,
)
from modelperf.data import train_test
from modelperf.models import BINARY_FEATURES, load_models
from modelperf.plots import (
    plot_estimated_vs_realized,
    plot_over_time,
    plot_psi,
    plot_psi_bins,
    plot_segments,
    use_style,
)

use_style()
gbm = load_models()["binary"]["GBM"]
reference = reference_and_pool().train
y_ref = reference["HasClaim"].to_numpy()
p_ref = gbm.predict_proba(reference[BINARY_FEATURES])[:, 1]
months = {s: simulate_months(s) for s in SCENARIOS}
last = {s: m[m["month"] == N_MONTHS] for s, m in months.items()}
names = list(SCENARIOS.values())


def fmt_p(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"= {p:.3f}"
```

**Question answered:** has the model's performance changed since it was
validated, and can we tell before the outcomes come in?

Every earlier page measured performance on a test set with known outcomes.
In production the outcomes arrive late. A claim may be reported weeks after
the accident and settled years later, so a pricing model's AUC or deviance for
this month's policies can only be computed long after the policies were
written. Meanwhile the portfolio changes: new distribution channels, new
vehicles, new regulation. **Drift monitoring** watches what *is* available
right away (the features and the model's predictions) for signs that
performance may have changed.

This page covers three tools, from simple to more ambitious:

- the **population stability index (PSI)**, which compares the distribution of
  one feature with its distribution in the reference data;
- a **domain classifier**, which looks at all features at once;
- **confidence-based performance estimation (CBPE)**, which estimates the
  model's AUC and log loss without any outcomes.

It also shows the kind of drift that none of them can see.

## Two kinds of drift

A model learns the joint distribution of features $x$ and outcome $y$, which
splits into two parts:

$$
P(x, y) = P(y \mid x) \, P(x).
$$

- **Covariate shift:** $P(x)$ changes, $P(y \mid x)$ doesn't. The portfolio
  contains different policies, but a given policy is as risky as before. A
  well-specified model keeps predicting correctly for each policy, though
  portfolio-level metrics can still move, because AUC and log loss depend on
  the mix of policies.
- **Concept drift:** $P(y \mid x)$ changes. The same policy is now more (or
  less) risky than the model believes. The model is wrong, and nothing in
  $x$ shows it.

Feature-based monitoring can only detect the first kind. Whether a detected
shift *matters* is a separate question.

## The setup: a year of simulated production

The test set is split in half. One half is the **reference**: labelled data
the model was validated on, as on every earlier page. The other half is a
pool from which we draw `{python} N_MONTHS` monthly **production batches** of
`{python} f"{BATCH_SIZE:,}"` policies each. Drift grows linearly: month 1 has
none, month `{python} N_MONTHS` the full effect. We monitor the GBM for
`HasClaim`. The split into halves is stratified by claim, fuel type, area and
age band, so that the segments the scenarios change start out alike in both
halves: differences between reference and production then come from the
simulated drift, not from the luck of the split.

```{python}
#| include: false
cov, ben, con = last["covariate"], last["benign"], last["concept"]
pool = reference_and_pool().test
rural_ref = reference["Area"].isin(RURAL_AREAS)
```

| Scenario | What changes by month `{python} N_MONTHS` | A plausible cause |
|---|---|---|
| Covariate shift | Young drivers are sampled more often: the average driver age falls from `{python} f"{reference['DrivAge'].mean():.0f}"` to `{python} f"{cov['DrivAge'].mean():.0f}"`. Risk *given* the features is unchanged. | A new online channel attracts young drivers |
| Concept drift | The features are unchanged, but the claim rate in the rural areas `{python} ", ".join(RURAL_AREAS)` (`{python} f"{rural_ref.mean():.0%}"` of policies) rises by `{python} f"{RURAL_CLAIM_INCREASE:.0%}"`. | More traffic on rural roads, or a run of storms |
| Benign drift | The share of diesel cars falls from `{python} f"{(reference['VehGas'] == 'Diesel').mean():.0%}"` to `{python} f"{DIESEL_SHARE:.0%}"`. The models barely use fuel type, and diesel and petrol cars have similar claim rates. | Diesel bans in city centres |

: The three simulated drift scenarios. {#tbl-scenarios}

A monthly monitoring job computes the following for each batch. The first
three blocks need only the features; the last needs the outcomes, which in
reality would arrive months later.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def monitor(batch: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    X, y = batch[BINARY_FEATURES], batch["HasClaim"].to_numpy()
    p = gbm.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    # Input drift: each feature, and all features together
    row = {f: population_stability_index(reference[f], X[f]) for f in BINARY_FEATURES}
    row["domain AUC"] = domain_classifier_auc(reference[BINARY_FEATURES], X)
    # Prediction drift
    row["score PSI"] = population_stability_index(p_ref, p)
    # Estimated performance (no outcomes needed)
    row.update({f"est. {k}": v for k, v in cbpe(y_ref, p_ref, p).items()})
    # Realized performance with standard errors (once the outcomes are in)
    loss = -(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))
    auc_boot = paired_bootstrap(auc_rank, y, {"GBM": p}, n_boot=200)["GBM"]
    row.update({
        "positive rate": y.mean(), "se positive rate": np.sqrt(y.mean() * (1 - y.mean()) / y.size),
        "AUC": auc_rank(y, p), "se AUC": auc_boot.std(),
        "log loss": loss.mean(), "se log loss": loss.std() / np.sqrt(y.size),
    })
    return row


results = {
    s: pd.DataFrame([monitor(b) for _, b in months[s].groupby("month")], index=range(1, N_MONTHS + 1))
    for s in SCENARIOS
}
```

## Population stability index

The PSI compares a feature's distribution in the current data with the
reference. Cut the feature into bins (deciles of the reference data for a
numeric feature, one bin per category otherwise), compute the share of
policies in each bin in both samples, $r_k$ and $c_k$, and add up

$$
\text{PSI} = \sum_k (c_k - r_k) \ln \frac{c_k}{r_k}.
$$

Each term is positive whenever $c_k \neq r_k$, so shifts in different
directions don't cancel. The PSI is the Kullback–Leibler divergence taken in
both directions, $\text{KL}(c \,\|\, r) + \text{KL}(r \,\|\, c)$. Credit-risk
practice gave it widely used rules of thumb: below 0.1 the distribution is
stable, 0.1–0.25 is a moderate shift, above 0.25 a major one.

Here are driver ages in the last month of the covariate-shift scenario:

```{python}
#| label: fig-psi-bins
#| fig-cap: "Driver age in the reference data and in the last month of the covariate-shift scenario, binned at the reference deciles. Each bin's contribution to the PSI is in the table below."
t_age = psi_table(reference["DrivAge"], cov["DrivAge"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
plot_psi_bins(t_age, ax=ax, xlabel="Driver age (reference deciles)")
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-psi-bins
#| tbl-cap: "PSI of driver age, bin by bin."
t_age.assign(**{"current − reference": t_age["current"] - t_age["reference"]})[
    ["reference", "current", "current − reference", "contribution"]
].T.round(3)
```

The youngest bins more than doubled and the oldest shrank, giving a PSI of
`{python} f"{t_age['contribution'].sum():.2f}"`, a major shift. Computing the
PSI of every feature in the last month of each scenario:

```{python}
#| label: fig-psi-features
#| fig-cap: "PSI of each feature in the last month of each scenario. Dashed lines mark the usual thresholds for a moderate (0.1) and a major (0.25) shift."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharey=False)
xmax = 1.1 * max(results[s].loc[N_MONTHS, BINARY_FEATURES].max() for s in SCENARIOS)
for ax, (s, name) in zip(axes, SCENARIOS.items()):
    plot_psi(results[s].loc[N_MONTHS, BINARY_FEATURES].astype(float), ax=ax, title=name, xmax=xmax)
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
r_cov, r_con, r_ben = (results[s] for s in ("covariate", "concept", "benign"))
psi_bm = r_cov.loc[N_MONTHS, "BonusMalus"]
```

- **Covariate shift:** driver age shifts strongly. So does the bonus-malus
  level (PSI `{python} f"{psi_bm:.2f}"`), because young drivers have not yet
  earned a bonus: shifting one feature shifts every feature correlated with it.
- **Concept drift:** every PSI is close to 0. The features really are
  unchanged, so feature monitoring has nothing to find.
- **Benign drift:** fuel type crosses the 'major' threshold
  (`{python} f"{r_ben.loc[N_MONTHS, 'VehGas']:.2f}"`), although, as the
  performance estimates below will show, it hardly matters to the model.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not a statistical test?
The two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (numeric features) or the chi-squared
test (categories) asks whether two samples come from *exactly* the same
distribution. With thousands of policies per month, it detects shifts far too
small to matter.

```{python}
#| include: false
b2 = months["covariate"][months["covariate"]["month"] == 2]
ks2 = ks_2samp(reference["DrivAge"], b2["DrivAge"])
psi2 = population_stability_index(reference["DrivAge"], b2["DrivAge"])
```

In month 2 of the covariate-shift scenario, driver age has a PSI of only
`{python} f"{psi2:.3f}"`, yet the KS test gives
p `{python} fmt_p(ks2.pvalue)`. Tests answer 'is there any difference?'; the PSI
measures *how large* the difference is, which is what monitoring needs.
:::

PSI has limits:

- It looks at **one feature at a time.** A change in how features combine
  (young drivers suddenly owning powerful cars) can leave every marginal
  distribution intact.
- **Binning matters.** Deciles of the reference data are the usual choice.
  Features with few distinct values, such as the bonus-malus level (more than
  half the policies sit at 50), get fewer bins.
- **Its thresholds are conventions**, not statistical results. With small
  batches, sampling noise alone can push the PSI past 0.1.

Applied to the model's predictions instead of a feature, the PSI measures
**prediction drift**. It has the advantage of summarizing all features in the
units that matter to the model; we return to it below.

## Domain classifier

To look at all features together, train a classifier to tell the two samples
apart. Label reference policies 0 and current policies 1, fit a model to
predict the label from the features, and measure its cross-validated AUC:

- **AUC ≈ 0.5:** the classifier can't tell the samples apart; no detectable
  drift.
- **AUC well above 0.5:** the samples differ, in a way the classifier has
  learned. Its feature importances show which features drive the difference.

Any classifier works; we use a gradient boosting machine, so interactions
between features are covered too.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drift-over-time
#| fig-cap: "Input drift over the year. Left: the largest feature PSI each month. Right: cross-validated AUC of the domain classifier (0.5: indistinguishable from the reference)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
max_psi = pd.DataFrame({n: results[s][BINARY_FEATURES].max(axis=1) for s, n in SCENARIOS.items()})
plot_over_time(max_psi, ax=axes[0], ylabel="Largest feature PSI", hlines={"major shift": 0.25})
axes[0].set_title("Largest feature PSI")
domain = pd.DataFrame({n: results[s]["domain AUC"] for s, n in SCENARIOS.items()})
plot_over_time(domain, ax=axes[1], ylabel="Domain classifier AUC", hlines={"no drift": 0.5})
axes[1].set_title("Domain classifier")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Both detectors tell the same story. The covariate and benign shifts grow
steadily, and the domain classifier reaches an AUC of
`{python} f"{r_cov.loc[N_MONTHS, 'domain AUC']:.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{r_ben.loc[N_MONTHS, 'domain AUC']:.2f}"` by the last month. The
concept drift stays invisible: the domain classifier hovers around
`{python} f"{r_con['domain AUC'].mean():.2f}"`, as it should when the two
samples come from the same distribution.

The domain classifier's AUC is a better single number than a list of PSIs: one
value per month, covering every feature and interaction. But like the PSI it
answers *whether the inputs changed*, not *whether the model got worse*. The
benign drift raises both alarms without affecting the model at all.

## Estimating performance without outcomes

Confidence-based performance estimation (CBPE) goes one step further: it
estimates the model's metrics directly. The idea is to trust the model's own
probabilities. If a policy has a predicted claim probability of 4%, then on
average it contributes 0.04 of a claim and 0.96 of a non-claim. Adding these
expected counts over the batch gives an **expected confusion matrix** at
every threshold, and from it an expected ROC curve and an **expected AUC**.
Other metrics follow the same way. For log loss, with $\hat q_i$ the probability
taken as the truth,

$$
\widehat{\text{log loss}} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_i \left[ \hat q_i \ln p_i
+ (1 - \hat q_i) \ln (1 - p_i) \right],
$$

and the expected claim rate is simply the average of $\hat q_i$.

This only works if the probabilities are **calibrated**, so CBPE first
recalibrates them on the labelled reference data: $\hat q_i$ is the observed
claim rate among reference policies with a prediction like $p_i$ (isotonic
regression, as for the CORP reliability curve on the
[calibration page](../binary/calibration.qmd)). Then:

- under **covariate shift**, $P(y \mid x)$ is unchanged, so calibration
  carries over to the new portfolio, and CBPE follows the real performance,
  even when it changes;
- under **concept drift**, the recalibration map is out of date, and CBPE
  keeps reporting the old performance.

Here is the estimate (line) against the realized value (points, with 95%
intervals) for each scenario and metric. In reality the points would only
appear months later.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cbpe
#| fig-cap: "Estimated (CBPE, no outcomes) against realized performance of the GBM, month by month. Rows: scenarios. Columns: claim rate, AUC, log loss. The dashed line is the value on the reference data."
metrics = {"positive rate": "claim rate", "AUC": "AUC", "log loss": "log loss"}
ref_values = {"positive rate": y_ref.mean(), "AUC": auc_rank(y_ref, p_ref), "log loss": log_loss(y_ref, p_ref)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(11, 8.5), sharex=True, sharey="col")
for i, (s, name) in enumerate(SCENARIOS.items()):
    r = results[s]
    for j, (m, label) in enumerate(metrics.items()):
        t = pd.DataFrame({
            "estimated": r[f"est. {m}"], "realized": r[m],
            "lower": r[m] - 1.96 * r[f"se {m}"], "upper": r[m] + 1.96 * r[f"se {m}"],
        })
        ax = axes[i, j]
        plot_estimated_vs_realized(t, label, ax=ax, reference=ref_values[m])
        ax.set_title(f"{name}: {label}")
        ax.set_ylabel("")
        if i < 2:
            ax.set_xlabel("")
axes[0, 0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
def change(r, col):
    return r.loc[N_MONTHS - 2 :, col].mean() - r.loc[:3, col].mean()  # last 3 months against first 3

rel = lambda r, col: change(r, col) / r.loc[:3, col].mean()
gap_con = r_con.loc[N_MONTHS - 2 :, "positive rate"].mean() / r_con.loc[N_MONTHS - 2 :, "est. positive rate"].mean() - 1

# Drivers aged 25 or under: actual ÷ expected claims in the production pool and in training.
def young_ae(d):
    d = d[d["DrivAge"] <= 25]
    r, e = d["HasClaim"].mean(), gbm.predict_proba(d[BINARY_FEATURES])[:, 1].mean()
    return len(d), r / e, np.sqrt(r * (1 - r) / len(d)) / e

n_young, ae_young, se_young = young_ae(pool)
_, ae_young_train, _ = young_ae(train_test().train)
```

Reading the rows:

- **Covariate shift:** the estimates move with the portfolio. Between the
  first and last three months, CBPE expects the claim rate to rise by
  `{python} f"{rel(r_cov, 'est. positive rate'):.0%}"` (young drivers claim
  more) and the AUC to *rise* by
  `{python} f"{change(r_cov, 'est. AUC'):+.3f}"`: a portfolio with a wider
  range of risks is easier to rank. The realized AUC follows
  (`{python} f"{change(r_cov, 'AUC'):+.3f}"`). A large drift in the inputs, and
  the model copes, even slightly improves. This is the case CBPE is built for.
- **Concept drift:** the estimates are flat, because nothing the model sees
  has changed, but the realized claim rate climbs: in the last three months
  it is `{python} f"{gap_con:.0%}"` above the estimate, and the realized log
  loss rises with it. The realized AUC falls by
  `{python} f"{-change(r_con, 'AUC'):.3f}"`: the rural policies, which the
  model rates as low risk, now have more claims, so its ranking is worse too.
  Every label-free method misses this scenario.
- **Benign drift:** estimated and realized metrics stay close to the
  reference throughout. The fuel-type shift that crossed the PSI's 'major'
  threshold is irrelevant to performance.

In the covariate-shift row, the realized claim rate does *not* rise as
estimated. That is the luck of a small group, not a flaw in CBPE. The batches
draw their young drivers from the same `{python} f"{n_young:,}"` drivers aged
25 or under in the pool, and these happen to have
`{python} f"{1 - ae_young:.0%}"` fewer claims than the model expects (A/E
`{python} f"{ae_young:.2f}"`, standard error `{python} f"{se_young:.2f}"`). On
the training data the model is well calibrated for this age group (A/E
`{python} f"{ae_young_train:.2f}"`). Because the scenario oversamples the same
young drivers month after month, their luck repeats every month instead of
averaging out.

More generally, the realized points scatter around the estimates, sometimes
by more than one might expect. With `{python} f"{BATCH_SIZE:,}"` policies and about
`{python} f"{BATCH_SIZE * y_ref.mean():,.0f}"` claims per month, the realized
AUC of a single month has a standard error of about
`{python} f"{np.mean([results[s]['se AUC'].mean() for s in SCENARIOS]):.3f}"`.
Realized metrics are themselves estimates: judge each against its interval,
as on the [model comparison page](../comparison/model-comparison.qmd), rather
than reacting to every dip.

::: {.callout-note}
## CBPE's assumptions
CBPE needs **calibrated probabilities**, which the recalibration on reference
data provides, and **no concept drift**, which it cannot check. It also
assumes the calibration learned on the reference data holds for every kind of
policy in the new portfolio: if the model is well calibrated overall but
miscalibrated for young drivers, a shift towards young drivers biases the
estimate. Treat CBPE as an early warning, not as a substitute for the
realized metrics once outcomes arrive.

For continuous targets the analogous method is **direct loss estimation
(DLE)**: fit a second model on the reference data that predicts each
observation's loss (squared error, deviance) from its features and
prediction, and average its predictions over the new batch. For pure premium,
where a few large claims dominate every loss, that second model has very
little signal to learn from, so we don't demonstrate it here.
:::

## Catching concept drift

Concept drift is only visible in the outcomes. The tools are those of the
[calibration page](../binary/calibration.qmd), applied as soon as outcomes
arrive: compare actual with expected claims (**A/E**), overall and by segment.
Once the outcomes for the last month of the concept-drift scenario are in,
splitting A/E by area points straight at the cause:

```{python}
#| label: fig-ae-area
#| fig-cap: "Actual ÷ expected claims per area in the last month of the concept-drift scenario, with 95% intervals. Expected claims are the GBM's predictions; 1 means the model is right on average."
p_con = gbm.predict_proba(con[BINARY_FEATURES])[:, 1]
areas = sorted(con["Area"].unique())
rows = []
for a in areas:
    s = (con["Area"] == a).to_numpy()
    y_a = con.loc[s, "HasClaim"].to_numpy()
    se = np.sqrt(y_a.mean() * (1 - y_a.mean()) / s.sum())
    rows.append({"actual": y_a.mean(), "lower": y_a.mean() - 1.96 * se, "upper": y_a.mean() + 1.96 * se,
                 "GBM": p_con[s].mean()})
ae = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=range(1, len(areas) + 1))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
plot_segments(ae, ["GBM"], ax=ax, ratio=True, xlabel="Area (A: most rural, F: most urban)", ylabel="Actual ÷ expected claims")
ax.set_xticks(ae.index, areas)
ax.get_legend().remove()
fig.tight_layout()
```

The rural areas `{python} ", ".join(RURAL_AREAS)` have clearly more claims than
the model expects. Areas D and E have about as many as expected; area F,
the smallest, is too noisy to tell either way. Two practical consequences:

- **Outcomes arrive gradually.** Claim *counts* are known within weeks or
  months, long before claim *costs* are settled. Monitoring claim frequency
  (as here) gives an early read; cost-based metrics such as deviance or Gini
  for pure premium follow much later.
- **Segment-level A/E needs volume.** A month of one segment is noisy; pooling
  several months, or using a cumulative A/E chart, makes slow drift visible
  sooner.

## What each method can see

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Last month of each scenario: what the monitoring methods report, and what really happened. Changes are the last three months against the first three."
def summary(r):
    feats = r.loc[N_MONTHS, BINARY_FEATURES].astype(float)
    return {
        "largest feature PSI": f"{feats.max():.2f} ({feats.idxmax()})",
        "score PSI": f"{r.loc[N_MONTHS, 'score PSI']:.3f}",
        "domain classifier AUC": f"{r.loc[N_MONTHS, 'domain AUC']:.2f}",
        "est. claim rate change": f"{rel(r, 'est. positive rate'):+.0%}",
        "realized claim rate change": f"{rel(r, 'positive rate'):+.0%}",
        "est. AUC change": f"{change(r, 'est. AUC'):+.3f}",
        "realized AUC change": f"{change(r, 'AUC'):+.3f}",
    }

pd.DataFrame({name: summary(results[s]) for s, name in SCENARIOS.items()})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
score_psi_max = max(results[s]["score PSI"].max() for s in SCENARIOS)
```

The score PSI deserves a second look. It never exceeded
`{python} f"{score_psi_max:.3f}"` in every scenario, far below any threshold,
even under the covariate shift that moved driver age by a PSI of
`{python} f"{r_cov.loc[N_MONTHS, 'DrivAge']:.2f}"`. The model's predictions
depend on many features, and a shift in one of them moves the score
distribution only a little. Prediction drift is a sensitive alarm only when
the shift touches the features the model relies on most.

| Method | Needs outcomes? | Detects covariate shift | Detects concept drift | Says whether performance changed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PSI per feature | no | yes, one feature at a time | no | no |
| Domain classifier | no | yes, including interactions | no | no |
| Prediction drift (score PSI) | no | when it affects the score | no | no |
| CBPE / DLE | no | yes | no | yes, under covariate shift |
| Realized metrics, A/E by segment | **yes** | yes | **yes** | yes, after a delay |

: Monitoring methods and what they can see. {#tbl-methods}

## Takeaways

- Outcomes arrive late, so production monitoring starts with what is
  available now: **features and predictions**.
- **Covariate shift** (new kinds of policies) shows up in the features.
  **Concept drift** (the same policies behaving differently) doesn't, and
  every label-free method misses it.
- The **PSI** measures how much one feature's distribution moved; the
  **domain classifier** checks all features and their interactions at once.
  Both detect *change*, not *harm*: a large shift can leave the model
  unaffected (benign drift), or even slightly improve its AUC (covariate
  shift).
- **CBPE** turns the model's calibrated probabilities into estimated metrics.
  It follows real performance under covariate shift and is blind to concept
  drift.
- The only defence against concept drift is to compare predictions with
  outcomes as they arrive: **A/E overall and by segment**, judged against
  sampling noise.
